title.narrative: WB Zimbabwe Socio Economic Transformation Fund (ZISET)
WB Zimbabwe Socio Economic Transformation Fund (ZISET)

description.narrative: Målet med multigivarfonden är att bidra til ekonomisk stabilitet och inkluderande tillväxt i Zimbabwe genom att stärka den privata sektorn för ökat jobbskapande, förbättra offentlig förvaltning samt öka samhällets motståndskraft.

The objective of the trust-fund is to promote economic stability and inclusive growth in Zimbabwe by strengthening the private sector to create jobs, improving public sector effectiveness and building climate resilience.

The ZISET TF will support the implementation of the World Bank Group´s new Country Engagement Note FY25-26 which is structured around four objectives:
(1) Reduce macroeconomic distortions and strengthen fiscal policy and economic governance,
(2) Strengthen the enabling environment for an inclusive and resilient private sector,
(3) Boost pro-poor social services and women´s empowerment, and
(4) Promote energy transition and resilience to climate change and disasters.
The specific development objective of ZISET TF is to promote inclusive growth and socio-economic resilience. The focus is on strengthening the conditions for citizens and private sector firms to benefit from and be resilient to shifts in a developing macroeconomic environment, as well as to withstand shocks, including those linked to climate change. The TF aims at supporting policy development and reforms to improve the enabling environment for private sector led economic growth, trade, and job creation, as we all as contribute to strengthening the systems for social protection for the poorest and most vulnerable.
ZISET activities are organized under two pillars, with inclusion of underserved groups, such as women, girls and the extreme poor as a cross-cutting priority, to tackle social exclusion and fragmentation.
Pillar 1. Supporting inclusive, private sector-led growth
Activities under this pillar will promote economic transformation and creation of quality jobs by strengthening the private sector enabling environment, enhancing firm capabilities and competitiveness, facilitating cross-border trade, and promoting financial sector resilience and inclusion. Supporting women-led businesses and addressing gender gaps in economic opportunities will be prioritized across intervention areas, including the selection of value-chains with high concentration of women entrepreneurs, active engagement with women-led business associations, and tailoring of interventions to account for women´s reduced mobility and higher caring responsibilities.
Key expected outcomes include:
(1) Lower costs and streamlined licensing and compliance requirements for private sector, particularly in priority sectors.
(2) Improved firm-level practices, enhancing productivity and competitiveness
(3) Streamlined and lower cost of cross-border trade clearance procedures and systems Improved access to finance
(4) Increased adoption of climate risk financial instruments
(5) Strengthen and operationalize a new Green Industrial Policy
Pillar 2. Building household resilience and womens inclusion
Pillar 2 aims to bolster the resilience of the poorest and most vulnerable households and populations by improving the targeting, coordination, and resilience of social programs. Focus areas include strengthening and improving the targeting system for social protection programs by designing and operationalizing a social registry system and expanding the registry´s coverage to 20 percent of the population. Improving the shock-responsiveness of social protection programs and designing an improved the targeting system based on poverty and vulnerability data is also foreseen. In addition, activities will promote positioning of the social registry as a service platform across sectors, programs and financing sources to enhance harmonization and coordination in the sector.
Key expected outcomes include:
(1) Strengthening the Government of Zimbabwe capacity for implementation of the social protection system
(2) Enhanced coverage of the social protection system
(3) Improved shock-responsiveness of the social protection programs
Depending on available funding to the TF, the ZISET also proposes to work on improving the design of and to pilot cash programs aimed at adolescent girls, as well as support activities that specifically target women micro-entrepreneurs to increase productivity, financial resilience and earnings.

1. Business Environment Reform: reduced burdens and stronger regulatory systems
Substantial progress has been made toward strengthening the enabling environment for private-sector led growth. Three major reform action plans in the beef, dairy and feedstock sectors were finalized and approved by Cabinet, directly reducing costs, duplications and compliance burdens, thereby supporting Objectives 1 and 2 of the program. These reforms have improved transparency and contributed to a more predictable regulatory landscape. They are also expected to particularly benefit women-led micro and small enterprises, which typically face higher regulatory barriers and mobility constraints. In addition, the reforms contribute to a more climate-resilient private sector by easing regulatory constraints that limit investment in climate-adaptive production and technologies. Institutional capacity has increased as well, with more than ten ministries and agencies trained in regulatory analysis, licensing reform and compliance-cost modelling.
- Cabinet-approved reforms reducing fees, permits and regulatory steps
- Compliance databases and cost models established for priority sectors
- Multi-agency capacity building completed
- Cross-border trade study for Victoria FallsLivingstone informing tourism and trade reforms
2. Competitiveness and Access to Finance: foundations for enterprise growth
Progress under this component has strengthened the conditions for inclusive private-sector growth. A large-scale horticulture BDS program, expected to reach at least 5,000 hubs and farmers, is being prepared to enhance firm-level practices, productivity and access to markets. Diagnostics on MSME bankability and SACCOs are informing future reforms to improve access to finance, while a digital finance pilot has been co-developed with regulators and fintechs.
- BDS framework prepared for 5,000 horticulture actors
- MSME bankability and SACCO diagnostics underway
- Digital finance pilot designed; correspondent banking conference planned
3. Social Protection Systems: strengthened targeting and program design
Significant advancements have been made toward strengthening the Governments capacity to deliver inclusive and shock-responsive social protection, in alignment with Objective 3. The ZISO harmonized questionnaire was piloted, validated, and finalized, preparing the groundwork for nationwide enumeration. Governments co-financing commitment for ZISO IT hosting demonstrates growing ownership. Furthermore, the new Zimbabwe Social Cash Transfer (ZSCT) has been designed to harmonize fragmented programmes and improve targeting. Work has also progressed on vulnerability assessment and the redesign of BEAM, including a cash-plus pilot for adolescent girls. These efforts collectively enhance the systems ability to respond to climate-related shocks while improving access to services for women, girls and other underserved groups.
- Harmonized questionnaire finalized; population-level enumeration prepared
- Government co-financing secured for ZISO IT upgrades
- ZSCT program designed with improved targeting
- Vulnerability assessment drafted; BEAM redesign initiated
Unexpected results
- The Victoria Falls-Livingstone study catalyzed new Zambia-Zimbabwe dialogue, opening opportunities for cross-border tourism and trade cooperation.
- Government began co-financing ZISO IT support earlier than anticipated, signalling stronger national ownership and improving sustainability.
- Presidential engagement significantly raised the visibility of business-environment reforms, helping to accelerate national momentum for regulatory simplification and creating favourable conditions for sustaining gender- and climate-responsive reforms beyond Sida's support.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
